title: Stochastic waterfall: pacing vs econ sketch
content:
Goal:
A compact, shareable sketch comparing three pacing strategies under a stochastic waterfall arrival process. Focus: p50/p90/p99 latency, throughput, and incremental cost-per-1k-queries. This is an exploratory working doc — not a final deck.

Context / why this matters:
- We see customer workloads with long-tail session bursts (waterfall bursts where a high-intent cohort triggers many parallel calls within ~30s).
- Standard autoscale + simple prewarm either overprovisions or misses the tail; need heuristics that trade a small steady increase in capacity for big tail reductions.
- This doc sketches numeric intuition and micro-visuals to use in the product discussion (Optimize + Console teams).

Experiment setup (sketch):
- Synthetic session generator: baseline steady rate 100 qps, waterfall bursts sampled as Poisson bursts with lambda=0.7 and burst-size distribution heavy-tailed (Pareto k=1.5, scale=20). Burst duration ~5-40s.
- Model profile: 8k context, medium-sized model (cost proxy = $0.00045 / request baseline), single-GPU slice throughput 60 qps, warm-up penalty 0.8s cold.
- Pacing strategies compared:
  A) on-demand autoscale (default): scale when queue > threshold, prewarm disabled
  B) conservative pacing: keep +15% headroom (steady extra capacity)
  C) reactive prewarm: aggressive warmup when burst detected (prediction window 2s), but scales back fast
- Observables collected: p50/p90/p99 latency (ms), successful throughput (qps), cost per 1k requests ($), warmup penalty impact.

Quick numbers (aggregated from short-run sim; indicative only):
+----------------------+----------+---------+---------+-----------------+
| Strategy             | p50 (ms) | p90 (ms)| p99 (ms)| $ per 1k reqs   |
+----------------------+----------+---------+---------+-----------------+
| A) on-demand         |  110     |  320    |  1450   |  0.45           |
| B) conservative +15% |  105     |  160    |  420    |  0.52 (+16%)    |
| C) reactive prewarm  |  120     |  140    |  280    |  0.49 (+8.9%)   |
+----------------------+----------+---------+---------+-----------------+

Notes on interpretation:
- On-demand has low steady cost but extreme p99 tail due to cold starts + queueing during waterfall peaks.
- Conservative headroom reduces tail dramatically at the expense of steady incremental cost (~+16% in this sim).
- Reactive prewarm achieves much of the tail reduction (p99 ~280ms) with lower steady cost than conservative, but p50 slightly worse (due to background prewarm churn) and occasional misses for very large bursts.

Mini chart: tail vs cost tradeoff (ASCII waterfall bars, longer = higher p99):
- On-demand  : p99 = ||||||||||||||||||||||||| (1450ms)   cost: [$]
- Reactive   : p99 = ||||||||| (280ms)                   cost: [$$]
- Conservative: p99= ||||||||||| (420ms)                 cost: [$$$]

Rough throughput picture during a representative burst (peak qps):
- infrastructure cap per GPU = 60 qps. Base demand = 100 qps across fleet (mult-GPU).
- Observed peak draw for single burst: 1200 concurrent requests across fleet for ~8s.
- On-demand: backpressure + 2-3s queue growth -> observed throughput hit ~88% of demand at peak (tail latencies spike).
- Reactive: 92% of demand satisfied, short-lived misses for extreme tails.
- Conservative: 99% of demand satisfied, minimal queuing.

Failure modes and sensitivity:
- Prediction window too small (<=1s): reactive prewarm misses many bursts -> p99 rises toward on-demand.
- Aggressive prediction increases CPU/GPU churn (slightly higher p50 variance).
- Pareto tail heavier (k < 1.5): conservative headroom becomes more cost-effective (amortizes avoided retries).

Open questions / things to validate with real traces:
- Real burst size distribution (we used Pareto; need 30 sample traces from customers across product lines).
- Cold-start cost model: our baseline $/request ignores chance of retries or partial output; need better mapping to billing units.
- Interaction with KV-caching: prefix hits dramatically reduce effective qps; simulate with 20/50/80% cache hit scenarios.

Suggested next steps (quick):
- Pull 2 weeks of high-burst client traces (GREP: "burst" or high-session-concurrency) and compute empirical burst-size CDFs. Owner: Markus. ETA: 1 week. (JIRA OBS-487)
- Implement small sim harness in repo branch (link in linked_artifacts). Run grid over prediction windows [1..5s] and headroom [+0, +5, +10, +15%]. Owner: Lena. ETA: 2w.
- Console/Optimize: mock UI widget showing "expected tail reduction vs cost" using this sketch numbers for initial feedback. Owner: PM-Optimize.

Notes-to-self / loose thoughts:
- Could we expose a composite knob: "tail-sensitivity" which maps to either conservative headroom or reactive prewarm config? That lets product surface the choice without exposing internals.
- Consider coupling reactive prewarm to per-tenant historical burst fingerprint (long-tail customers get conservative default).

References / links in text:
- Sim branch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1823 (prototype sim harness)
- JIRA OBS-487 (trace pull + analysis)

End of sketch. Expect to iterate once we have real traces.
